title: Anderson v. City of Bessemer City, North Carolina
lead: A trial judge found that Bessemer City rejected its only female applicant for Recreation Director because of sex. The Supreme Court held that the court of appeals had replaced permissible factual findings with its own view instead of applying clear-error review.

actors.name: Anderson
actors.role: Schoolteacher and unsuccessful applicant for Recreation Director

actors.name: Bessemer City
actors.role: Municipal employer defending its hiring decision

actors.name: Auddie Boone
actors.role: Only woman on, and chair of, the five-person selection committee

actors.name: Donald Kincaid
actors.role: Applicant selected by the four male committee members

proceedings: Trial court found Title VII discrimination and awarded backpay and fees; Fourth Circuit reversed factual findings; Supreme Court reversed unanimously, with two separate concurrences.
limits: This source transformation concerns the historical Rule 52(a) decision and does not verify current rule wording or subsequent treatment. The final mandate specified reversal, without a separate new-trial direction.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The city chooses a Recreation Director
paragraphs: Bessemer City sought a Recreation Director to manage facilities and develop athletic and other recreational programs. Its selection committee consisted of four men and chairperson Auddie Boone, a woman. Eight candidates applied. Anderson, the only female applicant, was a thirty-nine-year-old schoolteacher with social-studies and education degrees. Donald Kincaid was twenty-four and newly graduated in physical education.

The four men selected Kincaid; Boone voted for Anderson. Anderson believed sex explained her rejection and filed an administrative charge. Five years later, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission found reasonable cause. Conciliation failed, and Anderson received a right-to-sue letter before bringing a Title VII action in the Western District of North Carolina.

sections.title: The trial judge hears the hiring evidence
paragraphs: Anderson, Kincaid, and all five committee members testified. The judge found Anderson better qualified for the job’s broad responsibilities. Her experience included teaching and recreational supervision, hospital recreation, civic activities, bookkeeping, public speaking, and familiarity with sports, music, dance, and crafts. Kincaid’s strengths focused on athletics, youth basketball coaching, student teaching, and his physical-education degree.

The judge also found differential questioning and bias. One man said the work would be difficult for a woman and he would not want his wife doing it. Another recruited men but no women. Anderson faced serious questions about night work, travel, and her husband’s approval; male candidates did not face comparable questioning. Boone recalled a comment about Kincaid’s new bride, but the judge regarded it as facetious and credited Boone over competing accounts from male members.

The claimed reasons for choosing Kincaid were found pretextual. The committee had initially preferred Bert Broadway for experience despite his lack of a physical-education degree, rejecting him only when he would not relocate. Testimony also weakened the asserted superiority of Kincaid’s proposed programs.

sections.title: The trial judgment and appellate reversal
paragraphs: The judge first announced a discrimination finding in a memorandum, then requested expanded proposed findings from Anderson. The city lodged extensive objections, Anderson replied, and the judge entered formal findings differing substantially from her proposal. Because Anderson conceded that ordering her appointment would be inappropriate, the court awarded $30,397 in backpay and $16,971.59 in attorney’s fees.

The Fourth Circuit held clearly erroneous the findings about comparative qualifications, differential questioning, and bias. It also suggested that the preparation of findings justified close scrutiny. The Supreme Court reviewed both the proper treatment of proposed findings and the scope of clear-error review. Pullman-Standard v. Swint, the Court’s precedent treating discriminatory intent under Title VII as factual, made Rule 52(a) applicable rather than unrestricted review of a legal conclusion.

sections.title: A permissible choice between factual accounts must stand
paragraphs: Justice White explained that clear error requires a definite and firm conviction of mistake on the whole evidence. Appellate disagreement alone is insufficient. If the trial judge’s account is plausible on the complete record, choosing it over another permissible account is not clearly erroneous.

The standard also applies to documentary or physical evidence and factual inferences, not only witness demeanor. Trial judges’ factfinding expertise, the cost of duplicating trial, and the trial’s place as the principal factfinding event supported deference. Credibility choices received added protection because tone and demeanor matter. Even those choices remained reviewable when contradicted by objective evidence, documents, internal inconsistency, or facial implausibility. Choosing between coherent, plausible, externally uncontradicted accounts ordinarily could not be reversed merely because appellate judges preferred one witness.

The Court continued to criticize uncritical adoption of counsel’s proposed findings, particularly unsupported or conclusory ones. But adopted findings remained judicial findings reviewed for clear error. Here, the judge supplied his own framework, heard objections, and changed organization and substance. There was no basis to doubt considered judgment or impose a stricter standard.

sections.title: The trial findings survive that review
paragraphs: On qualifications, the appellate court emphasized athletics while the trial judge emphasized broader recreational management. Either view was plausible, but the trial court had chosen the latter. The appellate court could not substitute its own permissible preference.

Boone’s account of spouse-related questioning was ambiguous. She denied questioning Kincaid in the same context as Anderson, and tone could support finding her comment facetious. No reliable external evidence defeated the trial judge’s choice between plausible witnesses. Those findings, combined with reservations about women doing the job and recruitment directed only to men, supported bias. The fact that committee members’ wives had worked did not necessarily dispel it; the weight of that evidence belonged to the trial judge.

The Supreme Court disclaimed superior knowledge of events or the committee members’ minds. Applying review rather than independently reconstructing the hiring, it reversed the Fourth Circuit on March 19, 1985. All nine Justices agreed with reversal; eight joined White’s opinion. The mandate itself specified reversal, not a new damages award or new trial.

sections.title: Two Justices explain the limits of their agreement
paragraphs: Justice Powell joined the opinion and judgment but stressed that the ruling should not discourage comprehensive record review. The Fourth Circuit had examined the evidence carefully, and reasonable observers could think the trial judge mistaken. Nevertheless, the factual issue could fairly be decided either way, defeating clear error. Powell also noted the five-year administrative delay and stale recollections.

Justice Blackmun concurred only in the judgment, agreeing with most of the reasoning. He regarded the proposition about wholly documentary evidence as broad dictum unnecessary in a case involving extensive live testimony. Having previously accepted a different approach, he preferred to await a case presenting that question with focused briefing and argument.
